ideas.title: Priority-Aware Load Shedding Protects Revenue Paths
ideas.description: Tag requests at the gateway (`critical`, `standard`, `best-effort`) so overload sheds recommendation widgets before dropping checkout mutations.

example.title: Stopping a Retry Storm & Noisy Neighbor at the API Gateway
example.scenario: A buggy mobile SDK retried 429s in a tight loop while a slow analytics query degraded database latency, pushing gateway CPU to 100% and taking down checkout.
example.reasoning: Deploying an atomic Redis Lua token-bucket limiter per API key (returning `429` with jittered `Retry-After`) stopped the SDK flood, while AIMD adaptive concurrency limits + priority shedding dropped best-effort feed requests before checkout threads saturated.
example.lesson: Rate limiting bounds external demand per tenant; adaptive load shedding protects internal capacity when downstream dependencies slow down.

reflectionQuestions: Why does a Fixed Window Counter allow up to 2x the configured rate limit across a minute boundary?

learningJourney.title: Multi-Region Active-Active, Observability & Disaster Recovery
learningJourney.purpose: Design globally resilient architectures with explicit RPO/RTO targets, multi-region conflict resolution, W3C distributed tracing, and automated chaos drills.
learningJourney.explanation:
Single-region systems fail completely when an entire cloud region loses control-plane or backbone connectivity. Disaster Recovery starts by quantifying **RPO (Recovery Point Objective)**—maximum tolerable data loss (e.g., 0s for ledgers via synchronous quorum, <5s for feeds via async replication)—and **RTO (Recovery Time Objective)**—maximum tolerable downtime for DNS/Anycast failover.

**Active-Passive** keeps a warm standby region fed by async replication, simplifying consistency at the cost of failover lag and potential RPO loss. **Active-Active** serves writes in multiple regions simultaneously for local latency (<30ms) and zero-RTO failover, but requires either **home-region user pinning** (EU users write in `eu-west-1`, US users in `us-east-1`), **global consensus** (Spanner/CockroachDB paying cross-region RTT), or **CRDTs** (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) to merge concurrent updates deterministically without coordination.

Operating multi-region fleets requires end-to-end **observability**: propagate **W3C `traceparent`** headers across HTTP, gRPC, and Kafka; bound Prometheus metric cardinality (never put `user_id` or `request_id` in labels); use **tail-based sampling** to retain 100% of error and p99 traces; and continuously validate failover runbooks with **Chaos Engineering GameDays**.

ideas.title: Let RPO and RTO Drive Active-Active vs Active-Passive
ideas.description: Active-Active eliminates regional failover RTO for stateless tiers, but multi-region writes force either cross-region consensus latency or CRDT/home-region conflict rules.

ideas.title: Pin Users to Home Regions Before Reaching for Multi-Leader Writes
ideas.description: Sharding user state by `home_region` gives 99% of requests local-region writes and strong consistency while keeping another region warm for DR promotion.

ideas.title: Tail-Based Sampling Captures 100% of Errors Without Storage Bloat
ideas.description: Head-based 1% sampling drops 99% of rare p99 bugs. Buffer spans briefly at the OTel collector and keep every trace with an error status or high latency.

ideas.title: Untested Failover Plans Are Broken Failover Plans
ideas.description: Run scheduled GameDays (blackholing a region's DNS or draining an AZ) to catch hidden single-region dependencies like shared auth databases or stale DNS TTLs.

example.title: Surviving a Full Cloud Region Blackout Under 60 Seconds
example.scenario: A fintech platform ran Active-Passive DR, but during an unplanned `us-east-1` outage, manual runbooks took 45 minutes because a shared Redis session store and a 3600s DNS TTL prevented traffic from shifting to `us-west-2`.
example.reasoning: Re-architecting to Active-Active with stateless JWTs + regional Redis clusters, home-region Postgres pinning with <5s async replication, 30s health-checked DNS failover, and monthly chaos GameDays brought real-world RTO down to 42 seconds.
example.lesson: Eliminate cross-region runtime dependencies on the critical path and test regional evacuation continuously with chaos drills.

reflectionQuestions: What is the concrete trade-off between RPO = 0 across two continents and write p99 latency?
Why does putting `user_id` or `order_id` in a Prometheus metric label crash monitoring infrastructure?
How do CRDTs allow two disconnected regions to merge concurrent updates without a central coordinator?

advanced.finalSummary: Strong system design starts with capacity math and clear contracts, selects SQL or NoSQL and B-Tree or LSM storage to match real access patterns, protects hot paths with multi-tier caching and CDN edge delivery, decouples bursts via partitioned queues and transactional outboxes, powers discovery with inverted and spatial indexes, and enforces correctness and resilience under overload or regional failure with quorums, fencing tokens, adaptive rate limiting, observability, and tested disaster recovery.
advanced.summary: System design is the discipline of turning ambiguous product goals into scalable, fault-tolerant distributed architectures grounded in capacity math, API contracts, relational and NoSQL data modeling, caching hierarchies, distributed coordination, and storage engine internals.
advanced.keyTakeaway: If latency budgets leave no room for synchronous retries, system design is not memorizing buzzword diagrams; it is quantifying bottlenecks first, choosing explicit consistency and latency trade-offs, isolating fault domains, and keeping the architecture as simple as the workload allows.
